name: Lower Arrernte / Arrernt Imarnt
confidence_why: Breen 2001 and Koch 1997, 2014 give only the general Arandic rule (main stress on the first consonant-initial syllable, usually the second syllable of the word) and say nothing about Lower Arrernte itself, a nearly extinct language known mainly from Hale's two hours of tape, so any stress placement for it is an extrapolation from its relatives, not a description.

catalog_quote: [Breen 2001:55] The most widespread stress rule in Arandic, usually stated: main stress falls on the first vowel that follows a consonant, does not have a simple statement in terms of conventional syllables, but is: stress falls on the second syllable with VC(C) syllables. Henderson (1990) found also that plural and reciprocal morphology is sensitive to whether stems are monosyllabic or disyllabic, but the rule is straightforward only with the VC(C) model. || [Breen 2001:67, sec. 4.11] Lower Arrernte has also been called Lower Southern Arrernte and Alenyerntarrpe ... the name preferred by the most authoritative of the handful of partial speakers I worked with is Arrernt Imarnt, literally 'solid Arrernte'. The best material available on it is two hours of tape and associated fieldnotes by Hale. This language is characterised by extensive movement forward of rounding to consonant onset (written as u). || [Koch 1997:285] (SC10) Stress shift to second syllable: #'SS.. > #S'S.. Stress in Arandic is on the first syllable beginning with a consonant (i.e. (V)'CV). This reflects the second syllable of Pre-Arandic. || [Koch 2014:320] Word-stress in Warlpiri is on the first syllable; in Arandic language stress is usually on the first syllable with an onset, which usually means the second syllable of the word.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Arandic-wide rule as stated by Breen and Koch: main stress goes on the first syllable that has a consonant onset, i.e. on the first vowel preceded by a consonant. Since nearly all Arandic words begin with a vowel, this is normally the second (orthographic) syllable; in Breen's VC(C)-syllable analysis it is the second syllable. No source opened states the rule for Lower Southern Arrernte itself; Breen's own section on Lower Arrernte (2001:67) covers rounding and the velar glide only. Breen's wording 'most widespread' signals that not every Arandic variety follows it.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not stated for Arandic in Breen 2001 or for Lower Arrernte anywhere. Koch 1997:284 only notes that many Australian languages have penultimate secondary stress in four-syllable words (a historical remark); Koch 2014:320 mentions Warlpiri primary/secondary stress in loan adaptation, not an Arandic rule.
new_statements.exceptions: None for Lower Arrernte. Breen 2001 calls the rule 'the most widespread stress rule in Arandic', implying exceptions among Arandic varieties, but names none in the Lower Arrernte section; Breen 2001:53 (the text layer) notes surface VCV words transfer stress to the initial vowel in some varieties.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (phonological word / stem plus suffixes); citation-form data. The statement is a family-level generalisation over Arandic, not a first-hand description of Lower Southern Arrernte stress.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement is for the Arandic group as a whole (Breen 2001; Koch 1997; Koch 2014), not for Lower Southern Arrernte (lowe1436) specifically. Breen 2001 section 4.11 (p.67) is the only accessible description devoted to Lower Arrernte (also called Lower Southern Arrernte, Alenyerntarrpe, Arrernt Imarnt; Hale's 'Lower Aranda (from Dalhousie)'; AIATSIS C29) and it is silent on stress. Lower Arrernte is a separate branch from the Upper Aranda dialect chain (Hale 1962 via Koch 2001:72-73), so the family-level rule should not be attributed to it without a first-hand statement. Not to be confused with Southern Arrernte/Pertame or with Western Arrernte (west2441), for which Breen's rule is already catalogued.

sources.note: p.55 (PDF p.11), end of sec. 3: 'The most widespread stress rule in Arandic, usually stated: main stress falls on the first vowel that follows a consonant.. is: stress falls on the second syllable with VC(C) syllables.' This is stated for Arandic as a group. Sec. 4.11 'Lower Arrernte' (p.67, PDF p.23) is the only dedicated description of the language (rounding moved to consonant onsets, velar glide after /i/, based on Hale's two hours of tape and Breen's own work with 'a handful of partial speakers') and says nothing about stress.
